title: Mechanisms of Prompt-Induced Hallucination in Vision-Language Models

We then introduce misaligned prompts asking the model to “Describe the N + k N+k [objects] in the image,”, where k ∈ { 1 , 2 , … , 5 } k\in\{1,2,\ldots,5\} . Here, the offset k k serves as a discrepancy distance , measuring the magnitude of misalignment between the prompt and the visual input. We allow the model to generate long-form responses up to 75 75 tokens and use a rule-based algorithm to determine accuracy by extracting the first non-negated numerical reference in the response (e.g., excluding constructions such as “there are not eight waterlilies”). A PIH occurs when the model proceeds to describe N + k N+k objects without correcting the count, despite contradictory visual evidence. We first evaluate the baseline accuracy of LlaVA-OneVision, Qwen-VL and Janus-Pro on CountBench Paiss et al. ( 2023 ) . Table 6 breaks performance down by the number of objects. All models perform reliably at very small counts (2–4 objects), but accuracy declines as counts increase. Notably, there are sharp dips at 5 objects (e.g., LLaVA-1.6: 87.27% to 65.91%, QwenVL: 90.91% to 75.00%) and again at 7 objects (Janus-Pro: 87.72% to 55.56%, LLaVA-OneVision: 89.47% to 48.15%).
